longusamuscle.c: LONGUS a Muscle ofthe Cubit, ‘ which helps to extend the Arm forwards.
LONGUS, a Muscle of the Radius, serving to turn the Palm of the Hand upwards.
LONGUS, a Muscle of the Tarsus so called See Peroneas Primus.

longuscolli.c: LONGUS Colli, is a Muscle of the Neck which, arises partly tendinous, but chiefly fleshy, from the fore - part of the Eive Vertebra of the Thorax; and being dilated in its Middle to a fleshy Belly, is in - served to the fore - part of all the Vertebra of the Neck: This with its Partner asfting, bends the Neck right forward. Between this and the Scalenus lies the Rc m Internus Major.

loof.c: LOOF, or as they usually pronounce it, Luff, is a Term used in C ending of a Ship: Thus Leaf up, is too L U M Is to bid the Steers - man keep nearer to the Wind. T o loos into an Harbour, is to Sail into it, close by the Wind. To Spring the Luff, is when a Ship, that before was going Large before the Wind, is brought close, or as they fay claps close by the Wind. When a Ship fails upon a Wind, as they fay, that is, on a Quarter Wind, the Word of him that cons to the Steers - man, is, Luff l keep your Luff veer m more ! keep her to i touch the Wind ! have a care of the Lee - latch: All which Words signifie much the fame thing, and bid the Man at Helm to keep the Ship near the Wind. But on the contrary, if the Ship is to go more Large, or Right before the Wind, the Word is, - Ease the Helm ! No near ! Bear up !

LOOF - HOOK, is a Tackle aboard a Ship, with two Hooks to it; one of which is to hitch into the Cxengle of the Main and Fore - fail, and the other is to hitch into a certain Strap which is spliced into the Cbeffe - Tree, ands down the Saih Its Use is to succour the Tackles in a large Sail, that all the ftrels may not bear upon the Tack. Sometimes also ' tis used, when the Tack, is to be seized thefurer.
LOOF - TACKLE, or Luff - Tackle, is small Tackle in a Ship, lerving to lift all final ! Weights in or out of a Ship.

loop.c: LOOP of a Ship, is that part of her a - loft, which lies just before the Cheffe - trees j and hence the Guns that lie here are called her Loof - Pieces.

LOOP, in the Iron - Works at the Forge; is the Term for about of C. sse. of Iron which is melt - ed and broken off from a Sow in the Fire of the Pinery, and at last is brought into a Bloom. This work they call Shingling the Loop.

LOOP - HOLES, are Holes made in the Com - ings of the Hatches of Ships, and in their Bulk - heads to fire Muskets thro ’ in a close Fight; and the fame are they in the covert Defences of all For - tifications,

loome.c: LOOME: If a Ship appears big at Sea, when seen at a Distance, they fay she homes, or appears a great Sail.,
LOOME - GALE, is a gentle, easie Gale or Wind, in which a Ship can carry her Top - Sails a - trip: See Trip.

lord.c: LORD, by the Writers of the Law, is divided into Lord Paramount, and Lord Mesne. Lord Mesne, is he that is Owner of a Mannor, and by Vertue thereof hath Tenants holding of him in Fee, and by a Copy of Court - Roll, and yet hold - eth himself of a superior Lord, called Lord Para - mount. Also, he is Called Lord in Gross, that is, a Lord having no Mannor, as the King in relpedt of of his Crowft. And there it a Case wherein a Pri - ate Man is Lord in Gross; as when a Man make's a ' Gift in Tail of all the Land he hath, to hold of him, and dieth; his Heir hath but a Seigniory ih Gross.

lordosis.c: LORDOSIS, by some Writers, is the Term for the bending of the Backbone forwards in Chil - dren, &c. , LOTION, a Term uled by forfie Chymifts ast Phhfmacal Write'rs, signifying only the washing of any Medicine ih Water. Some also call Remedies, which are between a Fomentationztid a Bath, and Which are uled to wash the Head, or any Part af - seated, by this Name of Lotion.

lowerflank.c: LOWER Flank., or Retir'd Flank; See Flank, A Term in Fortification.

loxodromiques.c: LOXODROMIQUES, is the Art or Way of oblique Sailing by the Bpmb, which always makes an equal Angle with every Meridian; i. e. when yon fail, ' neither difeClIy under the Equator, nor under one and the fame Meridian, but obliquely or across them. Hence the Table of Rhumbs, or the Traverse Table of Miles, with the Difference of Longitudes and Latitudes, by which the Sailor may practically find his Course, Distance, Latitude or Longitude, is by Sir j, Moore, and others, called by this Name of Londrimipues j and such Tables as serve truly and expeditiously to find the several Re - quifites, or resolve the Cafes of Sailing, are called Loxodromical Tables.

lozenge.c: LOZENGE, is that Figure in Heraldry which the Geometers call a Rhombus, i. e. a Parallelogram, whose Angles are oblique, but Sides all equal; and the Distance between the two obtuse Angles al - ways equal to the Length of one of the Sides. Thus, In which it differs from the Fusil which fee. In this Figure all unmarried Gen - tlewomen and Widows do bear their Coats of Arms; because, as some fay. Was the Figure of the Amazonian Shield j or, as others, because ’ tis the Ancient Figure of the Spindle.

lucidacor.c: LUCID A Cor once, a fix ’ d Star of the Second Magnitude, in the Northern Garland; whose Long - tude is deg. min. Latitude deg. min. pight Ascension deg. min.

lucidalyra.c: LUCID A Lyra, a bright Star of the first Mag - nitude, in the Constellation Lyra; whose Longitude is deg. min. Latitude deg. min. Bight Ascension deg. min. and Declination deg. ’ min.

luciferous.c: LUCIFEROUS, that which brings Light; a Word used by my Lord Bacon, and feme other Na - turalifts, for such Experiments in Philosophy as do not so much enrich a Man, as inform and enlighten his Mind about some Phyfiological Truth, or Spe - cubation in Physicks.

luesvenerea.c: LUES Venerea, Morbus Gabicus, the French Pox, is a malignant and contagious Distemper, commu - nicated from one to another by Coition, or other impure Contadfc; proceeding from virulent Matter, and accompanied with many ill Symptoms, such as Gonorrheas, with the Falling - off the Hair, Spots, Swellings / Ulcers, Pains in the Bones, &c.

luffaseaterm.c: LUFF, a Sea Term; the fame with Loof, which fee.

lumbago.c: LUMBAGO, is a Pain in the Muscles of the Loins, which Blanchard takes to be logged with Scorbutick Matter; so that the Patient is forced to stand upright, being not able to fit down without great Pain.

lumbarisvena.c: LUMBARIS Vena, a Vein arising from the de sending Trunk of the Cava, and is not always one but often two or three on each side, which they dC vide into the Lumbaris Superior and Inferior - they are bestowed on the Muscles of the Loins, and on the Peritoneum.

lumbarisarteries.c: LUMBARIS Arteries, are by feme said to come from the Aorta, unto all the Parts of the Loins, and to the Marrow of the Back - bone; fending as many Branches to its Joints, as there are Holes in it.

lumbricalmuscles.c: LUMBRICAL Muscles, are with some Anaro - mists those Four Muscles which serve to move the Fingers or Toes, and afe so called from their Worm - like Form.

lumbricales.c: LUMBRICALES, feu Vermiculares, are Muscles of the Fingers, so called from their Figure, being not much unlike the common Earth - Worms; they are also called Flex pres primi internodii i digitorum - from their Use. Those probably perform those mi - note Motions of the Fingers, when the second and third Intermodes are euryaced by the two si treated of L UN of Muscles j and therefore used in playing on Must - cal Instruments, and may be thence named Mufculi Fidicinalcs.

lumbricalispedis.c: LUMBRICALIS Pedis, is a Muscle of the lesser Toes, springing from the internal Part of the Os Cates's; and becoming tendinous, joins with the Tendons of the Preforans in the middle of the Sole of the Foot; then dividing it self into Four ( as it were ) distinct fleshly Muscles, they all become ten - dinous at their Insertions to the internal Parts of each lesser Toe, laterally next the Great Toe.

luminaries.c: LUMINARIES. The Sun and Moon are so cal - led by way of Eminence, for their extraordinary Lustre, and the great Proportion of Light that they afford us.

lunacornea.c: LUNA Cornea, is a tough insipid Mals, almost like Horn, made by pouring warily on Chtyftals of Silver ( which Chrystals were made by dissolving that Metal in good Aquafortis or Spirit of Nitre ) either Spirit of Salt, or a strong Brine made of com - mon Salt and Water. The Mixture is dried, and then brought to Fusion in a Crucible, ora Glass Vial; where, after it hath been kept a little while so, it turns into this Shape, which the Chy mills call Cornea Luna. In which Process ’ tis very remarkable, that tho ‘ a Solution of Silver be commonly one of the worst of Bitters, and Spirit of Salt have a very four and acid Tast, yet the Union ofthefe together produces a Body perfedlly insipid; which plainly ( hews that Taste depend on Mechanical Principles, ' [ and are va - rious, according to the various Textures of Bodies.

lunarymonths.c: LUNARY Months, are either Periodical, Syno - dical, or Illuminative; which see in their proper Places.

lunarcycle.c: LUNAR Cycle: See Cycle of the Moon.

lunations.c: LUNATIONS of the Moon, are the Times be - tween one New Moon and another: And this is greater than the Periodical Month by two Days and five Hours; and is called the Synodical Months con - siding of Days, Hours, and of an Hour.

lunesorlunula.c: LUNES, or Lunula, in Geometry, are Figures in the Form of a Crescent or Half - Moon, made by the Arks of two interfering Circles; as in the sol - lowing Figures the Space L is called a Lune. PROPOSITION I. . The Quadrature of Hippocrates his Lunes, I fay, the Triangle T, is equal to the two Lunes L, and L.

lunettesinfortification.c: LUNETTES, in Fortification, ar e ' Evolopes Countergardes, or Mounts of Earth call up before the Curtain, about five Fathom in Breadth, where - of the Parapet takes up three. They are usually made infDitches full of Water, and serve tb the fame purpose as False Braies. These Lunettes are com - pos ’ d of two Faces, which from a Re - entring Angle and their Platform being only Twelve Foot Wide, is a little raised above the Level of the Water, and hath a Parapet three Eathom thick.

lunulas.c: LUNULAS, the feme with Lunes; Which fee.

lupia.c: LUPIA, is a Tumor, or Protuberance, about as big as a small fort of Bean j some take it for a Meliceris, others sot a Ganglio. Blanchard.

lupusasouthernconstellation.c: LUPUS, a Southern Constellation, confuting of two Stars.

lupus.c: LUPUS, a sort of Canker in the Thighs and Legs. Blanchard.

lust.c: LUST. If a Ship bed either to Starboard or Port, the Seamen sey that she hath a Lufi that way; and they sey so, tho ’ it be occasioned only by the Shoot - ing of her Ballast, or by the unequal flowing of things in her Hold. Tho ’ ’ tis more properly seid of a Ship, when she is inclined to heel any way, upon the Ac - count of her Mold or Make.

lutation.c: LUTATION, is a cementing of Chymical Ves - self close together.

lute.c: LUTE ( in Chymistry ) is that wherewith the Chymifts join together the Necks df the Retorts and Receivers, or wherewith they coat over the Bodies of Glass Retorts, to see them from being melted in very Violent Fires. The following Composition Lemery commends as good Lute. Take of Sand, Dross of Iron and Pot - ters Earth in Powder, of each five Pounds; Horse dung cut small, a Pound; powdered Glass and Sea - felt, of each tour Ounces. Temper all these well with Water, and then with the Pali coat the Retorts as far as to half the Neck j or use it to lute toge - ther ( as they call it ) the Necks of the Retorts and Receivers, When ’ tis dry, ‘ twill be exceeding hard; and therefore when you would separate the Vessels, you must - wet it first - well with exceeding wet Cloths. The Lute which Lemery used himself, was only two parts of Sand, and one of Clay, tempered to - gether in Water: Which will do very well to join the Nofes of Retorts, and their Receivers in the Distillation of Volatile Spirits, &c. When you distil by the Alembick, or Veflca, or Copper Body, with its Head and Serpentine, a wet Bladder will serve very well to lute the Jundures of the Vessels. But when corroding Spirits are to be distilled, ’ twill be better to use the following Lute Take fine Flower Slack ’ d Siack ’ d - lime, of each an Ounce j Potters Earth, or Powder of Pots, half an Ounce. Make a moist Paste of these with Whites of Eggs, well beaten before with a little Water, and this, will flop exceeding close, N. B This may be very well ufedto stone the Cracks that will often happen in Glass Vessels and there must be three Lays of the Paste bound on with Paper. Mr. Boyle recommends on Experience for this Iaft Purpose, the following Composition, Good Quick - lime and Scrapings of Cheele pounded in a Mortar, with as much Water as will just bring the Mixture to a Soft Paste; then spread it on a piece of Cloth, and apply it, as Occasion requires.

luxationaterminchyrurgery.c: LUXATION, a Term in Chyrurgery, is the Dislocation, displacing, or putting any Bone or Joint out of its Place.

luxatorexternus.c: LUXATOR Externus, a Muscle so called: See Ext emus Auris.

lycanthropiababieshydropbobica.c: LYCANTHROPIA, Babies Hydropbobica, a Madness proceeding from the Bite of a mad Wolf, wherein Men imitate the howling of Wolves. Blan - chard

lygmosthehickets.c: LYGMOS, the Hickets, is a convulsive Motion of the Nerves, which spread up and down; the Gul - let;, returning after short Intermifllons; It proceeds L Y N ' ' from some troublesome Matter that vellicates the Oesophagus. Blanchard.

lympha.c: LYMPHA, is a dear limpid Humour, confuting of the Nervous Juice and of Blood, which being continually separated by the Glandules, is at last discharged into the Blood again by Vessels peculiar to it. The Lympha comes not immediately from the Blood, or Nervous Juice, as some think, but it is the Superfluity of each; which Was more than enough for the Nourishment of a Part, like the Marrow in Bones. It is taken sometimes for that Water which flows from the Pricking of Nerves and other Wounds; and which does not really flow from the Nerves themselves, but from the Lympha - tick Vessels which are cut and wounded. Blanchard.

lympheducts.c: LYMPHEDUCTS, are slender pellucid Tubes, whose Cavities are contrabled at small and one - qual distances by two oppofire Semi - lunar Valves which permit a thin and transparent Liquor to pass thro ’ them towards the Heart, but which are fliut like Flood - gates on its returning. They rife in all parts of the Body, but after what man - ner needs no great dispute; for without doubt all the Liquids in the Body, excepting the Chyle, are separated from the Blood in the fine Capillary Vessels by a different Pipe from the common Cha - nel in which the reft of the Blood runs: But whe - ther this Pipe be longer or no longer than the thickness of the Coat of the Blood - vessel, whether it be visible or invisible, it is Full A Gland whilst it suffers some parts of the Blood to pass thro ’ it " denying a passage to others. Now the Glands that separate the Lympha are of the smallest kind, being invisible to the sines Microscopes; but their Excretory Duds, the Lymphatic Vessels, unite with one another, and grow larger as they ap - roach the Heart; yet they do not open into one common Chanel, as the Veins do; for sometimes we find or more Lymphafouds running one by another, which only communicate by foort inter - mediate Duds, or which unite and immediately divide again. Tn their Progress they always touch at one or two conglobate or vesicular Glands, in to which they discharge their Lympha. Sometimes the whole Lymphtedud opens at several places in - to the Glands, and sometimes it fends in only two or three Branches whilst the main Trunk passes over and joyns the Lymphteduds arising from the opposite side of the Glands, exporting again the Lympha to their common Receptacles. The Glands of the Abdomen which receive the Ly - phazduds from all the parts which it contains as likewise from the lower Extremities, are the Gain - dunce Inguinales, Sacra, Lumbares, Mefenterica and Hepatica all which fend out new Lympha duds which pour their Lympha into the Recepta - culum Chyli, as those of the Chest, Head and Arms do into the Duftus Yhoracicus, Tueular and clavian Veins. The design of the " LymphsdJta emptying themselves into the Conglobate Glands seems to be, that the flow Lympha may receive a new Velocity from the Elastick Compression of the Fibrous Cells of thole Glands, whose Fabrick resembles that of the Spleen; and therefore they f are improperly called Glands, because they sea - rate no Liquor from the Blood. lypyria.c: LYPYRIA, is the Term some Writers give to a kind of Fever attended with an EryJjpelas, or Cho - lerick Inflamarion of the Stomach and Guts; and tho ’ the inward Parts of the Body feel very hot, yet the outward ones are very cold. Blanchard.

lyratheharp.c: LYRA, the Harp, a Constellation in the Nor - thern Hemisphere, consisting of Stars. i - - i - if. - jib j;.

lacerta.c: LACERTA, is a word used in Doomsday - Book, and signifies a Fathom.

laches.c: LACHES, in the Law - sense, seems to signifie SUcknefs or Negligence, as appears from Littleton, Sel. and, where Laches of Entry is no - thing else but a negled of the Heir to enter; and io perhaps comes from our English word to Lack j unless from the French Lafeher or Lafche.

lachrymatories.c: LACHRYMATORIES, were small Earthen Vessels wherein the Tears of the weeping Friends that surviver were reposited and buried with the Allies and Urns of the Dead.

lad.c: LAD, is a Lade or Lath, from the Saxon La - than, signifies an Assembly or Court of Justice; and from hence the Annual Court at Dym - Church, by Bpmney - Marsh in Kent, for the Eledion of a Bailiff and other Officers is called Dym - Church - Lath to this Day.
LAD, from the Saxon Ladidn, also signifies a Purgation by Try al and in the Laws of K. E - thelred there is frequent mention of the Lada Sim - flex, Triple, and Plea.

lafordswick.c: LAFORDSWICK, in the old Saxon, is the Betraying of, or Infidelity to a Lord and Mailer. Tis mentioned in the Laws of Canutus, c.. and those of Henry I. c..

lag.c: LAG A, is, a word used for Law in Magna Car - ta and hence comes Dane Lage, Saxon Lage, Mercbn Lage, &c. as also

lagedayumorlagh.c: LAGEDAYUM or Lagh - day, that is, a Law - day, or day of open Court: Hence also a Lages - Man is Homo Legalis; and this word Lage - Man is frequently used in Doomsday - Book, and in the Laws of Ed. the Consessor.

ladenlagena.c: LADEN, Lagena, in ancient times was a Mea - sure containing fix Scxtarii. Vid Fleta,.. c.,. and Charta Ed.. m.,. n. z.

lahslitelagjlite.c: LAHSLITE, Lagjlite, Laghjlite, is used in the Laws of Hen. I. c. - for a Transgression of the Law; and sometimes for the Punilhment there - unto belonging.

lammasday.c: LAMMAS DAY, quasi Lamb - mas, is our first of Augufi, and on this day the Tenants which for - merly " held Lands of the Cathedral Church in York, were bound by their Tenure to bring a Lamb alive into the Church, at High - mass..

landirecti.c: LANDI RECTI, in the Saxons time, were such Services and Duties as were laid on those that held Land. These were Obligations, which from their Number were called T rinoda NeceJJitas, and were Exp edition, Burgh - bote, and Brig - bote. These were not called Servitia because not Feodal Ser - vices arising from the Condition of the Owners but by this name Landirebla, Rights that charged the very Land, whether polfeft by Churchman or Layman.

lapse.c: LAPSE, is the omission of a Patron to present to a Church within fix Months after voidable; on which negiedr. Title is given to the Ordinary to Collate to the said Church.

lashite.c: LASHITE, was a common Forfeiture in the time of the Danes; it was Ores, each Ore was about d. Sterling. Vid. Seldcn Hist. Tythes. Tho ” some fay, the On ? was in value about Pence, and that of them made the Libra or Pound.

last.c: LAST, in general signifies a Burden, and par - titularly a certain Weight or Measure: As a Last of Pitch, Tar, or Allies is Barrels; a Last of Hides or Skins is Dozen; a Last of Codfilh is Barrels; a Last of Herrings is Cades, ' or Ten Thousand; a Last of Corn is ten Quarters; a Last of Wool is Sacks j a Last of Leather is Dickers, and every Dicker is o Skins j a Last of unpack ’ d Herrings is Barrels.

LAST, in the Marffies of the East of Kent, also is a Court held by Jurats, and summoned by the two Bailiffs thereof, wherein they make Or - ders, lay and levy Taxes, &c. for the prefervati - on of the Marlhes.
LAST - HERE, is he to whom the Land comes by Escheat, for want of lawful Heirs; which is sometimes the Lord of whom the Land is fields and sometimes the King.

lastageorleft.c: LAST AGE or Left age, is a Custom exadled in some Fairs and Markets, to carry things where one will, faith Bast all but sometimes ’ tis taken al - so for the Balaft of a Ship; and as some fay, ’ tis properly a Custom paid for Wares fold by the Last.

Perhaps the Ridings in Toif - Jhire are so called corruptly from Tithirgs or T ridings, as ’ tis sometimes written. Matters that could not be determined in the Hundred Court, were brought to the Trithing, where the principal Men of or more Hundreds being assembled by the Authority of the Lath Reeve or Trithing Reeve, did decide and determine it; but if they did not, it went further to the County Court.

latrocinium.c: LATROCINIUM, in feme old Charters, is used for the Liberty of Infang - thief, or the Privi - lege of adjudging and executing Thieves.

laudimium.c: LAUDIMIUM, in the Civil Law, is the th part of the value of Land or Houses paid by the Proprietor to the new Tenant, by way of Emghy - teufis, as an Acknowledgment upon Invefiitures, or for being put into possession.

launder.c: LAUNDER, is a Trench cut in the Floor Foot long and Foot over, with a Turf for a Stopper at one End, to let the Water ( which comes along with the bruised Ore from the Coffer of a Stamping Mill in the Tin - works run away while the Ore finks to the bottom. See Tin.

laurets.c: LAURETS, were pieces of Gold coined in the Year, with the King ’ s Head laureated on them. I here was a /, piece marked with xx, one of io. marked x. and one of marked v.

lead.c: LEAD. The Lead Mines in Somersetshire are at Men dip, which is a place all Mountainous, but the Hills are of unequalHeights; ’ tis Barren and Cold, and in some places Rocky: the Ridges of the Hills run confusedly, but molt East and Weft, and not many parallel one with another. The Sur - face is heathy, Ferny and Furzy; it feeds Sheep all the Year; and young Beasts, Horses and Colts at Spring and Fall. The Soil is Red and Stony, but no way Clayie, Mar ley or Chalkey. The Stones are either of the nature of Fire - stones or Lime - stones. The Trees have their Tops burnt, and the Leaves and their outside discolored and scorched with the Wind; and they grow to no considerable bigness. The Stones which are wailit out by the Brooks and Springs are reddiffi and ponderous. The Country is more troubled with Thunder and Lightning, Storms, Nodlurnal Lights and Fiery Meteors, than other parts f. the Coun - ty. - When they have gotten the Ore they heat it small, then waste it clean in a running Stream, and then lift it in Iron Rudders, after which they make an Hearth or Furnace either of Clay or Fire - done, which they fet in the Ground, and upon it build. their Fire which is lighted with Charcoal, and. con - tinged with young Oaken Gadds: ' tis blown with Bellows by Mens treading upon them, and after the Fire is lighted and the Fire - place hot, they throw their Lead Ore upon the Wood which melts down into the Furnace and then with an Iron Ladle they take it out, and on Sand call: it into what form they please. Phil. Trans. N.. . In Phil. T rays. N.. you have this further ac - count. The Veins of Lead have been found to run up into the Roots of Trees without apparently alter - ing them. White, Yellow and mixr Earth, are Lea -, ders to the Country or Place where the Ore lies and changeable Colours do always encourage their hopes.: Sometimes they dig Fathom deep be - fore they meet with any Stones other while when Vol. II. a Stony Realty is at top, they meet Ore just under the Swerd or Surface of the Grass which Ore hath gone down Fathom. A Biack. Stone is an ill sign, and leads to Jam, as ' they call it, that is, a thick Bed of Stone that hinders their Work - y a grey, clear and dry one they account the belt '. They seldom meet with any Damps. If in sinking they come to wet moorish Earth, they ekpeft a and to be closed up with Rocks. Their n earn eft to the Ore, they guess by short brittle Clay; for they don ’ t think or find a tough Clay to be leading, as they call it; that is, diretfting towards Ore.. Sometimes the Ore lies ' Stole or shallow, and ' then it is or Fathom, more or less, before they hit it. They follow a Vein inclining to some depth, when it runs away in little flat Finns. When the Stones part it then they find a Vein: again. heir Draughts are or Fathom til ! ' they come to a Stone, where they call: a Side - Draught, called a Cut. Then they sink plufrii ? a - gain or Cuts one under another: they find Ore at Fathom. Their belt Rcakj are North and South; East and Weft are good, tho ’ not so deep. The Groove is Foot long and z - Foot broad, till they meet with Stone, and then they carry it as they can. The Groove is supported by Timber a piece as big as one ’ s Arm will support ro Tun of Earth. The Timber there Masts long, they have known it lie Years, and after that will serve in new works; it is tough and black, and being ex - posed a few Days to the Sun and Wind grows lo hard that an Ax will scarce cut ' it. For the supply of Air, they have Boxes of Elm, exactly closed, of about Inches in the clear, by which they carry it down Fathom and more - but when they come at Ore and need an Air - stoat, they sink it or Fathom distant, of the fame fafliion with a Groove, to draw as well Ore as Air. They make use of Leathern Bags, holding or Gallons a piece, to free them from Water, which are drawn up with Ropes. If they find a Swallet, they drive an Adit upon a level till it is dry. If they cannot cut the Rock, they use Fire to anneal. it, laying on Wood and Coal, and contriving ' thA Fire so that they can leave the Mine before, opera - tion begins; and they find it dangerous to enter again before it be quite cleared of the Smoak which hath killed some. Their Beetles, Axes and Wedges, &c. useless so: hardened as to make a deep impression on the Head of an Anvil, are not fit for their use and yet they sometimes break them in an Hour; others last or Days, as it happens. They work in Frocks and Waftcoats, by Candle - light if of Tal - low ) or: to the Pound, each of which lasts Hours if they: have Air enough. A Vein being loft, they drive or Fathom in the Breast, as the nature of the Earth directs them. They hand out their Materials in Elm Buckets drawn by Ropes; the Buckets hold about a Gallon. Their Ladders are of Ropes. The Ore sometimes runs in a Vein and some - times is dispersed in Banks - -, it lies often be - tween Rocks: Some of it is hard, some miller. Many tunes they have branched Ore in the Spar. About the Ore there is a Spar and Chalk and ano - ther Substance which they call Crootes, which is a meally white Stone matted with Ore, and fast. The Spar is white, transparent and brittle like Glass, The Chalk white, and heavier than any Stone, A z The LEG LEV The Vein lies between the Coats, and is of dise - rent Breadths; it breaks off sometimes abruptly in an Earth, which they call a deading Bed; and after a Fathom or two may come again to. keep the fame Point. It te minutes sometimes in a Rock called a Fire - stone, and sometimes in a dead Earth, Clayie without either Croote or Spar. The cleareft and hardest Ore is the belt, of which hundred weight makes about a Tun of Lead. The Hearth for melting the Ore is about Foot high, fet on Timber, to be turned about as a ’ Wind - mill, to avoid the Smoak on a shifting Wind it holds half a Bushel of Ore and Coal: There is a Sink on the side of the Hearth into which the Lead runs, and it holds about It Hundred. They have a Bar to stir the Fire, a Shovel to throw it up, and a Ladle heated red hot to call out the melted Metal. Once melting is enough and the bell, which is the heaviest, melts first. There is a Flight ( as they call it ) or Steam in the Smoak, which falling on the Grass, poisons those Cattle that eat of it. The Workmen find the taste of it ( when the Smoak flies in their Faces ) to be sweet upon their Lips; brought home and laid in their Houses it kills Rats and Mice. What of this Flight falls upon the Sand, they gather up to melt on a Flag - Hearth, and make Shot and Sheet Lead of it.

leveling.c: LEVELING, is the art of finding a true Horizontal Line, or the difference of Ascent or De - seen between any two Places, in order to drain Moors, Marfhes and Moraffes, &c. or to convey Water from place to place. The Instruments made use of you will find under the word Level in Vol. I. and Pendulous Level in Vol. If. The Method of Proceeding in the Art of Level - ling is, or may be much the fame, let the Instru - ment be the common Water Level, that of Spirit of Wine, or the new Pendulous one. The most commodious and expeditious way is to provide two Station Staves of square Deal, like Rulers, a - bout or o Foot in length. Let every Foot be divided into o parts, and. each of those into o more; so each small division will be the too part of a Foot. On each of these Staves there must be a Vane to Aide up and down, and with a Screw in she back - part to fallen it to any height on the Staff. ) L i G Staff. The fore - side of the Vane or Sight Ihould be painted white, or covered with white Paper, with a ‘ black. Line drawn across it lengthways; ha - ving then two assistants to hold theie Staves up - right, and to Aide the Sights up and down, sup - posing you were to find the difference of the Heights of any two places, as of A and B: if one Station will do, place the Level in the middle be - tween the places, and having by the Bubble or o - otherwise fet it truly Horizontal, look back to the first place, till your aififtant Hiding the Vane up. and down for you there on the Staff, you can see the black Line thereon cut or covered by the cross Hair in the Telescope; and then let him mark the height of that black Line above the Ground on the Divisions on the Staff. Then turn the Telescope about and look towards your other Aififtant at B, till you can see the Black Line on the Vane or Sight on his Staff coinciding with the cross Hair in the Telescope: and let him also note how high his Black Line is above the Ground; if his Number be the fame with the former, the Places are on a level, or of the fame height; other - wife that where the greatest Number is, is the highest; and the difference between the Numbers shews how much. But if the Places are so far asunder, or have ob - staples interposing, that you can ’ t do it at one Sta - tion, as is usually the case, then you must do it at as few more than one as you can, and you must keep an account o the Numbers on the Staves at all your Stations; putting the Back Station in one Column, and the Fore Station in another, with a ( Column for the Number of their Stations in the middle; in this or such like form. Where all the Back Sta - tions make together.. or fix Foot and. of a Foot, and all the Fore Stations make,.. or Feet and. of a Foot. And the difference between those Numbers being.. or Feet. of a Foot is the ex - cess in height of the last place above the first. N. B. In leveling of Ri - vers, you must fet the Black Line of the Sight in the first Backward, and in their last Fore Station, just to the Edge of the Water: And then you may take the Intermediate Stations, any where, a Mile off from the River, V. in the Meadow adjoining, for it will all come right at last.

lungs.c: LUNGS. These Organs of Relpiration are seated in the middle of the Cavity of the Thorax and divided into ? Lobes by the Mcdiaftinum, of which, the left, is ordinarily subdivided into more, The Figure of both Lobes together refer - ble the Foot of an Ox or Cow, being a little con - cave between the Lobes, where they embrace the Heart; and behind, where they lie upon the Verte - bra: But before, where they touch the Sternum and Bibs, they are Convex. The Colour of the Lungs in a Pcetus is of a pale Red; but after the Air hath once entred into them they lose their Red, and remain always Pale; yet in Adult Persons, they are often variegated with the one and the other. They are tied to the Sternum by the Mediajli num before, and to the Vertebra by the Pleura be - hind, when it rises from the Vertebra to the Heart by the Vena and Arteria Pulmondris; and some - time aodfew L U N L U times to the Pleura, where it covers the. Ribs, par - titularly in the left side, and especially after a Pleurifie. The Lobes ' of the Lungs are covered with a double Membrane; of which the External is a production of the Pleura: and the Internal, not only covers immediately the substance of the Lungs, but its inner Lamina fill up the Interstices which are below the Bunches of the small Lobes with little vesicular Cells: The fine Capillary Blood - Vessels, are so thick upon rhis Membrane, that it seems to be nothing but a Net - work of Veins and Arteries. The Substance of the Lungs is composed of an infinite number of little Lobes of various Figures and Magnitudes; but their Surfaces are so adapted to one another, as to leave but very few, and those small Interstices. These Lobes are disposed like so many Bunches of Grapes upon the sides of the Bronchia. Each little Lobe contains within its own proper Mem - brane an infinite number of little orbicular Vessels, which leave small Interstices between them; and which are full of small Membranes, like those which tie the Lobes together.
